q.q: A root-filled tooth with a post has a narrow, isolated deep pocket, a recurrent sinus tract and a J-shaped radiolucency along the root. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: An isolated narrow deep pocket with a J-shaped (halo) radiolucency on a root-filled tooth, often with a post, is the classic picture of a vertical root fracture.

q.n: The candidate said several questions were about vertical root fracture. The recall named only the topic; the question and options were written around it.

q.q: A vertical root fracture is confirmed in a single-rooted, root-filled tooth. What is the management?
q.e: A vertical root fracture in a single-rooted tooth is hopeless, so the tooth is extracted. In a multirooted tooth, the fractured root alone can sometimes be amputated.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S01-Q7-O)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q7-O cites: Berman LH, Hargreaves KM, eds. Cohen’s Pathways of the Pulp. 12th ed. Vertical-root-fracture diagnosis and management section.

q.q: An impacted lower third molar: the space between the distal of the second molar and the ramus is smaller than the crown's mesiodistal width. What is its Pell and Gregory class?
q.e: Pell and Gregory classify by ramus relationship. Class I has enough space for the whole crown, Class II has less space than the crown width, and in Class III the tooth is entirely within the ramus. Positions A–C describe depth relative to the occlusal plane.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16
q.r: Where to read more: Hupp JR et al. Contemporary Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. Classification of impacted teeth.

q.q: An infant with natal teeth has an ulcer on the ventral surface of the tongue. What is it?
q.e: Riga–Fede disease is a traumatic ulcer on the ventral tongue caused by natal or neonatal teeth rubbing during suckling. It is managed by smoothing the incisal edge or, if needed, removing the tooth.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16

q.q: A patient has clubbing of the fingers. Which investigation should be requested?
q.e: Finger clubbing is most often linked to chronic lung disease (lung cancer, bronchiectasis, fibrosis) or cyanotic heart disease, so a chest X-ray is the first investigation.

q.q: When is a band-and-loop space maintainer indicated?
o: Loss of a primary second molar before the first permanent molar erupts
Premature loss of a single primary molar on one side
Loss of several primary molars on both sides with erupted incisors
q.e: A band and loop holds space for a single missing primary molar on one side. A lingual arch is used when several teeth are lost on both sides with the permanent incisors erupted. A distal shoe is used when the second primary molar is lost before the first permanent molar erupts.

q.q: A cephalometric ANB angle of 7° indicates which skeletal classification?
q.e: The ANB angle classifies the skeletal pattern: about 2–4° is Class I, more than 4° is Class II, and less than 0–2° (negative) is Class III.

q.q: A patient on stable warfarin needs one simple extraction. The INR taken within 24 hours is below 3.5. What do you do?
o: Stop warfarin for 5 days before extraction
Continue warfarin and extract with local hemostatic measures
q.e: With a stable INR up to 3.5, simple extractions go ahead without stopping warfarin. Use local measures: sutures, a hemostatic dressing and tranexamic acid mouthwash. Stopping warfarin risks thromboembolism.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q653)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q653 cites: Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme. Management of Dental Patients Taking Anticoagulants or Antiplatelet Drugs. 2nd ed. 2022; Little and Falace's Dental Management of the Medically Compromised Patient. 10th ed. Anticoagulant therapy.

q.q: A patient on warfarin needs an extraction, but the INR is above 4. What do you do?
o: Postpone the extraction and refer to the physician to adjust the INR
Stop warfarin yourself and extract the next day
q.e: Above the safe range (more than about 3.5–4), the extraction is deferred and the physician adjusts the anticoagulation. The dentist never stops or changes warfarin without the prescriber.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S10-Q653)

q.q: A 30-kg child needs ibuprofen at 10 mg/kg per dose. What is the single dose?
q.e: 10 mg/kg × 30 kg = 300 mg, every 6–8 hours. The usual pediatric range is 4–10 mg/kg per dose, which is 120–300 mg for a 30-kg child.
q.c: Consistent with a related Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 question (S10-Q213)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S10-Q213 cites: American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry. Useful Medications for Oral Conditions. Latest revision 2025.
q.n: The recall said "calculate ibuprofen for 30 kg"; the 10 mg/kg dose is the usual one used in these questions.

q.q: Which burs are used to gain endodontic access through a porcelain-fused-to-metal crown?
o: A carbide bur through both porcelain and metal
A diamond bur through the porcelain, then a carbide (transmetal) bur through the metal
A diamond bur through both layers
q.e: Diamonds cut ceramic with less chipping, and carbide (or transmetal) burs cut metal efficiently, so they are used in sequence.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S01-Q140)

q.q: A dentigerous cyst surrounds an impacted tooth that won't be kept. What is the treatment?
o: Enucleation with curettage and removal of the tooth
q.e: Most dentigerous cysts are treated by enucleation (with curettage) and removal of the associated tooth. Marsupialization is reserved for very large cysts, or when the tooth is to be kept and guided into eruption.
q.c: Confirmed: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 gives the same answer (S10-Q534)

q.q: A dark-skinned woman has a rapidly appearing pigmented oral lesion; histology shows dendritic melanocytes throughout an acanthotic epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Oral melanoacanthoma is a benign, often fast-growing pigmented lesion, most common in young dark-skinned women. It shows acanthosis with dendritic melanocytes and often resolves after biopsy. Acantholysis (loss of cell cohesion) is the hallmark of pemphigus.
q.c: Candidate's answer; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16. ⚠ Check the histology word.
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. Oral melanoacanthoma.

q.q: A child has an inflamed distal shoe on one side where the first permanent molar is now erupting; on the other side the first molar has not erupted. What replaces the distal shoe?
o: Reverse band and loop (banded to the erupted first molar)
Leave it and remove the distal shoe without replacement
q.e: Once the first permanent molar has erupted, the distal shoe is no longer needed for guidance. Space is held with a reverse band and loop from the molar to the primary first molar. A lingual arch needs both first molars erupted.
q.c: Candidate's answer; Not covered in Rafi' Al-Maqam 16
q.r: Where to read more: Dean JA, ed. McDonald and Avery's Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent. Space maintenance.

q.q: A patient has a moon face. Which test confirms the suspected condition?
q.e: Moon facies points to Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol), which is confirmed by measuring cortisol (e.g., 24-hour urinary free cortisol or a dexamethasone suppression test).

In the groove between the mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canals

o: Warthin tumor of the submandibular gland
q.e: The parotid lies in front of the ear, and pleomorphic adenoma is the most common parotid (and salivary) tumour. Warthin tumour also occurs in the parotid, but not in the submandibular gland.

q.q: An old denture is worn overnight; the palate under it is diffusely red. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Diffuse erythema limited to the denture-bearing area, with overnight wear and poor hygiene, is denture stomatitis (Candida). It is treated with denture hygiene, removing the denture at night and antifungals.

q.q: A patient needs new dentures but the mucosa is inflamed from the old one. What do you do before the final impression?
o: Treat the tissue first (tissue conditioner or leave the denture out) and take the impression after it heals
Prescribe antibiotics and take the impression the same day
q.e: Impressions of inflamed, distorted tissue give an ill-fitting denture. Rest the tissue first with a temporary tissue conditioner or by leaving the denture out (at least 24 hours), and take the impression once it has recovered.

q.e: A high restoration makes the jaw deviate to avoid the contact, which strains the muscles and the TMJ. Check with articulating paper and adjust the occlusion.

q.q: What does using warm water when mixing an impression material (e.g., alginate) do?
o: Shortens the working and setting time
q.e: Heat speeds the setting reaction, so warm water shortens working and setting time. Cold water is used to lengthen working time.

q.e: Immediate severe pain, rapid swelling, bruising and bleeding into the canal during irrigation is the classic hypochlorite accident.

q.q: How is a sodium hypochlorite accident managed?
o: Stop irrigating, reassure, cold compresses then warm, analgesics, and antibiotics if infection risk; refer if the airway is affected
Inject more sodium hypochlorite to neutralize it
Continue irrigating to dilute the hypochlorite
q.e: Management is supportive. Stop and irrigate gently with saline, give analgesia, use cold compresses first then warm ones, and prescribe antibiotics if infection risk or tissue necrosis is likely. Reassure the patient and review. Refer urgently if the swelling threatens the airway.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; consistent with Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 hypochlorite questions (S01-Q6-L)
q.r: Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 S01-Q6-L cites: Guivarc’h M, et al. Sodium hypochlorite accident: a systematic review. J Endod. 2017;43(1):16-24. doi:10.1016/j.joen.2016.09.023.
q.n: The recall named only the topic; the question and options were written around it.

q.q: How are sodium hypochlorite accidents prevented?
o: A large open-ended needle wedged in the canal
A side-vented needle 1–2 mm short of working length, never bound in the canal, with gentle pressure
Irrigating with high pressure past the apex
q.e: Use a side-vented needle placed loosely, short of working length, moved up and down with light pressure, under rubber dam. Avoid binding and forceful injection, especially with open apices.

q.q: What is another name for hypercementosis?
q.e: Hypercementosis (cementum hyperplasia) is excessive deposition of normal cementum on the root, giving a bulbous root.

q.q: Which finish line is the most hygienic?
q.e: Supragingival margins are easiest to prepare, record, finish and clean, and they don't irritate the gingiva.

q.q: Two crown preparations are shown: one has a finish line that runs straight across the proximal under the papilla, the other rises interproximally to follow the gingival scallop. Which is better?
o: The straight finish line under the papilla
The finish line that rises interproximally, following the gingival scallop
q.e: The margin should follow the scalloped CEJ and gingiva. A straight margin goes too deep interproximally under the papilla, invading the supracrestal attached tissues (biologic width).

q.q: A patient returns the day after a surgical extraction with persistent bleeding. The site has sutures in place, and no medical history is given. What is the most appropriate management?
q.e: Post-extraction bleeding in a healthy patient is managed locally first: pressure, local hemostatic agents and tranexamic acid. FFP and transfusion are for coagulopathy or major blood loss.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning. ⚠ The recall didn't give the answer; some keys pick re-exploring the site.

q.q: A dentist has a percutaneous needlestick injury from a needle contaminated with blood from an HIV-positive patient. What is the risk of HIV transmission?
q.e: The risk after a percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood is about 0.3% (hepatitis C about 1.8%, hepatitis B up to 30% in the unvaccinated). Post-exposure prophylaxis is still started as soon as possible.

q.q: A woman has one-sided headaches that come in episodes over months, with nausea and vomiting. What is the diagnosis?
q.e: Migraine: unilateral throbbing headache lasting hours, with nausea, vomiting and light sensitivity. Paroxysmal hemicrania gives many short (2–30 min) orbital attacks a day with tearing, and responds to indomethacin.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning
q.r: Where to read more: Okeson JP. Bell's Orofacial Pains.

q.q: A space analysis shows a required space of 25 mm and an available space of 26 mm. What is the result?
q.e: Available space minus required space: +1 mm, so there is spacing. A negative result means crowding.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning
q.r: Where to read more: Proffit WR et al. Contemporary Orthodontics.

q.q: You are placing an amalgam restoration, and 0.5 mm of dentin remains over the pulp. What do you place?
q.e: With about 0.5 mm of remaining dentin and no exposure, a glass ionomer (RMGI) base protects the pulp. Calcium hydroxide is reserved for less than 0.5 mm or a near-exposure, then covered with GIC.
q.c: Answer worked out by reasoning; confirmed by Rafi' Al-Maqam 16 (S02-Q82). ⚠ Some keys say calcium hydroxide.

q.q: A 20-year-old has simple caries in tooth 24 limited to enamel, so you prepare it without local anesthesia. During the preparation the patient feels pain although you are still in enamel. What is the most likely cause?
q.e: Enamel spindles are odontoblastic processes that cross the DEJ into the inner enamel, so cutting there can hurt even though the bur is still in enamel. Tufts and lamellae are hypomineralized or organic defects with no cellular processes, and rods are acellular.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Sturdevant's Art and Science of Operative Dentistry, 7th ed., ch. 1, p. 6 (the bank cites the 5th ed., ch. 2, p. 21).

q.q: A 9-year-old has an unerupted, impacted maxillary left permanent canine. A periapical is taken, then a second one with the tube shifted horizontally to the distal (shown). On the second film the canine moves in the same direction as the tube (distally). Using the buccal object (SLOB) rule, where is the canine?
o: In the center of the maxillary sinus
In the soft tissue outside the bone
On the buccal side of the arch
On the lingual (palatal) side of the arch
q.e: SLOB: Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal. An object that moves in the same direction as the tube is lingual (palatal); one that moves opposite to the tube is buccal.

q.q: A 48-year-old has an asymptomatic lesion on the dorsum of the tongue: a well-defined red patch with irregular white keratotic borders that has been there for some time and doesn't rub off. Potentially malignant lesions are considered. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: A mixed red-and-white patch that can't be rubbed off is erythroleukoplakia (speckled leukoplakia). It carries a higher malignant risk than plain leukoplakia, so it needs a biopsy. Pure erythroplakia is red only; lichen planus is usually bilateral with Wickham striae.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology.

q.q: A 50-year-old asymptomatic patient has a routine panoramic radiograph showing multiple well-defined mixed radiolucent–radiopaque lesions in all four quadrants, in tooth-bearing areas, with no pain, swelling or expansion. The teeth are vital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: Multiple mixed lesions in several quadrants of the tooth-bearing jaw, with vital teeth and no symptoms, are florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (typically middle-aged Black women). It needs no treatment, and biopsy is avoided because the sclerotic bone infects easily.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank

q.q: An infection-control supervisor sees that the sharps container is almost full, and the assistant keeps filling it, thinking it must be completely full before disposal. When should a sharps container be discarded?
o: Only after one full year of use
When the color of the container fades
q.e: Sharps containers are closed and replaced when about ¾ full (at the fill line). Overfilling makes needlestick injuries more likely.

q.r: Where to read more: CDC. Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings.

q.q: A 30-year-old has pain and mild swelling in the anterior maxilla between 11 and 21, with slight palatal fullness in the incisive region. A well-defined, unilocular, symmetrical midline radiolucency of about 6 mm lies between the roots of the central incisors, which are not non-vital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: A midline, well-defined radiolucency between vital maxillary central incisors, with palatal swelling in the incisive papilla area, is a nasopalatine (incisive canal) duct cyst. A periapical granuloma needs a non-vital tooth.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology.

q.q: During complete denture fabrication, the dentist measures the distance between facial landmarks to help establish the vertical dimension. Which instrument is used?
q.e: The Willis gauge measures facial distances (e.g., base of nose to chin, or pupil to the corner of the mouth) when setting the vertical dimension. A Boley gauge measures small lengths such as tooth or acrylic dimensions, and an Iwanson caliper measures the thickness of wax or metal in the laboratory.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Zarb G et al. Prosthodontic Treatment for Edentulous Patients.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q7).

q.q: An assistant receives a sealed sterilization pouch for a surgical procedure. Its chemical indicator should have changed color but is still blue after the cycle. What should she do?
o: Wipe the instruments with alcohol and use them
Use them because the pouch is sealed
Report it and send the instruments back for reprocessing
q.e: An unchanged chemical indicator means sterilizing conditions weren't confirmed, so the instruments count as non-sterile. They are reprocessed and the problem is reported, so the sterilizer can be checked (including with a biological indicator).
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank

q.q: A 5-year-old has severe localized pain on the lower right. The primary mandibular right second molar has deep caries with pulp exposure and a fluctuant buccal swelling, without facial cellulitis, lymphadenopathy or fever (37.1 °C). What is the immediate treatment for rapid pain relief?
o: Open the pulp chamber (unroof it) for drainage, then pulpectomy or extraction once the acute phase settles
Topical benzocaine on the mucosa and dismiss the patient
Extraoral incision through the cheek under general anesthesia
Amoxicillin for 7 days, with no local treatment until it is finished
q.e: A localized abscess on a primary molar without systemic signs is drained locally: opening the pulp chamber gives immediate relief. Antibiotics alone are not enough and are reserved for spreading infection or fever. Once the swelling settles, decide between pulpectomy and extraction.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: McDonald and Avery's Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent, 10th ed., ch. 3, p. 40.

q.q: A healthy, asymptomatic 20-year-old has multiple radiolucent jaw lesions on a panoramic radiograph. His father had a similar condition with surgical removal of multiple jaw lesions. A hereditary syndrome is suspected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: Multiple odontogenic keratocysts in a young patient with a family history point to nevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome, which is autosomal dominant. Look also for basal cell carcinomas, bifid ribs, palmar pits and falx calcification.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q10).

q.q: A 40-year-old bruxer has discomfort in 37 and 47, which have amalgam restorations with open margins, heavy wear facets and areas of enamel out of occlusion. What is the most appropriate treatment?
q.e: In a heavy bruxer, failing restorations on mandibular molars are best replaced with full-metal crowns: metal resists fracture, needs the least reduction and is kind to the opposing teeth, and esthetics don't matter in this area.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q11).

q.q: A 33-year-old asymptomatic patient has an incidental, well-defined, homogeneous dense radiopaque mass in the posterior mandible, like cortical bone, with smooth borders, no radiolucent rim, no relation to the roots and no expansion, unchanged over time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: A dense, uniform radiopacity like cortical bone, with no radiolucent rim and no attachment to a root, is an osteoma. A cementoblastoma is fused to a root and has a radiolucent rim; sclerosing osteomyelitis is diffuse and ill-defined. Multiple osteomas suggest Gardner syndrome.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q12).

q.q: A 29-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, needs treatment for a serious condition that may end the pregnancy. The physician discusses it only with her husband and proceeds on his consent, without involving her. She is upset when she finds out. What has been violated?
q.e: A competent adult patient decides about her own treatment; consent from a spouse cannot replace hers. Leaving her out of the decision violates her rights and autonomy.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Saudi Commission for Health Specialties. Professionalism and Ethics Handbook.

q.q: A 6-year-old girl has difficulty articulating 't' and 'd'. A short, thick lingual frenum runs from the floor of the mouth to the tip of the tongue, giving a heart-shaped notch on protrusion. What is the diagnosis and is surgery indicated?
o: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie); frenectomy/frenuloplasty, because it limits tongue movement and speech
q.e: A short lingual frenum reaching the tongue tip is ankyloglossia. In an older child, surgical release is recommended only when it causes speech problems or local issues, which is the case here.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: McDonald and Avery's Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent, 10th ed., ch. 3.

q.q: A dentist has a needlestick injury from an HBV-positive patient. He completed the hepatitis B vaccine series and has documented adequate anti-HBs response. What is the management for hepatitis B?
o: No further hepatitis B prophylaxis is needed
q.e: A documented vaccine responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) is protected and needs no HBIG or booster after exposure. The exposure is still reported and the wound washed.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: CDC. Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q15).

q.q: A 52-year-old is missing 14–17, 34–37, 44–47 and all third molars, so there are no posterior occlusal stops. How should the jaw relationship be recorded to mount the casts?
o: Record blocks (bite blocks) and a facebow transfer, recorded in centric relation
q.e: Without posterior stops, maximum intercuspation can't be found reliably, so record blocks are used to register centric relation, and a facebow mounts the maxillary cast correctly before the case is planned.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q16).

q.q: Compare a three-unit FPD replacing a maxillary canine with one replacing a mandibular canine (abutments: lateral incisor and first premolar, good support, Class I with canine guidance). Which is true?
o: The maxillary FPD doesn't satisfy Ante's law
The mandibular FPD doesn't satisfy Ante's law
The maxillary canine FPD receives more (outward) lateral forces
The mandibular canine FPD receives more lateral forces
q.e: A canine pontic lies outside the line joining the abutments. On the maxilla the forces push the pontic outward (labially), against the inside of the arch curve, so a maxillary canine FPD is under more stress than a mandibular one, where forces push inward.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics.

q.q: A 33-year-old has shortened anterior and posterior teeth (shown), with flattened occlusal surfaces, worn incisal edges and reduced vertical dimension of occlusion. There is no trauma. What is the most likely cause?
q.e: Flat, matching wear facets on opposing teeth come from tooth-to-tooth contact, i.e., attrition, often driven by bruxism. Usually the VDO is kept by continued eruption, but heavy generalized wear can reduce it.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank; see the ⚠ note
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q18). ⚠ 'Parafunctional habits only' is a near-miss: bruxism causes the contact, but 'only' rules it out. The bank's answer names the mechanism.

q.q: A 46-year-old has fractured labial porcelain on recently placed PFM crowns on the mandibular anterior teeth. Posterior teeth are missing and the overbite is deep. The crowns were comfortable at first and fractured during normal function. What is the most likely cause?
q.e: With missing posterior teeth and a deep bite, the anterior crowns take loads meant for the posterior teeth. This occlusal overload chips the porcelain.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics.

q.q: In a Class II (occlusomesial) preparation in a primary mandibular first molar, which pulp feature must be considered to avoid exposure?
o: A small pulp chamber relative to the crown
Large, high pulp horns close to the surface (especially the mesial horn)
q.e: Primary molars have thin enamel and dentin and large pulps with high pulp horns; the mesiobuccal horn of the mandibular first molar is especially prominent, so preparations stay shallow.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: McDonald and Avery's Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent, 10th ed.

q.q: Which hand instrument is used to sharpen line angles and create retention features in dentin when preparing for a cast gold inlay, and to bevel enamel margins?
q.e: The angle former is a monangled chisel with its edge at an angle: it sharpens line and point angles and forms retention grooves in dentin for gold restorations, and it can bevel enamel margins.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Sturdevant's Art and Science of Operative Dentistry.

q.q: A lateral incisor with a non-restorable crown fracture is extracted, and the patient wants a good-looking temporary FPD while the definitive treatment is planned. Which pontic design suits this esthetic area?
q.e: An ovate pontic sits in the fresh socket, supports the papillae and gives the most natural emergence. Placed in a provisional right after extraction, it shapes the healing tissue for the final restoration.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: Rosenstiel SF et al. Contemporary Fixed Prosthodontics.
q.n: From Dr. Fhd's November 2026 recall quiz (Q22).

q.q: A 1-month-old girl has feeding difficulty and airway obstruction, with severe mandibular micrognathia, a U-shaped cleft palate and glossoptosis. What is the condition, and what feeding technique helps?
o: Pierre Robin sequence; bottle feeding with the infant upright and gentle forward pressure on the mandible
Treacher Collins syndrome; force-feeding lying flat
Down syndrome; tongue reduction at 1 month
q.e: Micrognathia, glossoptosis and a U-shaped cleft palate make up the Pierre Robin sequence. Feeding upright, with forward pressure on the mandible, keeps the tongue forward and the airway open.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank
q.r: Where to read more: McDonald and Avery's Dentistry for the Child and Adolescent, 10th ed.

q.q: A dentist must follow professional standards, obey the laws governing practice and decide by ethical principles. Which best describes a doctor's fundamental responsibilities?
o: Morals, ethics and professionalism (in that order)
q.e: The stem names the three: professional standards (professionalism), the regulations (laws) and ethical principles (ethics). 'Morals' are personal values, not one of the framework's duties.

q.q: A 62-year-old man has diffuse dull jaw pain, fatigue and weight loss over a few months. A panoramic radiograph shows multiple well-defined 'punched-out' radiolucencies in both jaws without sclerotic borders, with cortical thinning. The teeth are vital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: Multiple punched-out radiolucencies without sclerotic rims in an older adult with bone pain, fatigue and weight loss suggest multiple myeloma. Refer for blood tests and serum/urine protein electrophoresis.

q.q: A 45-year-old has a painful, itchy, one-sided rash of grouped vesicles on a red base in a dermatomal pattern, extending to one side of the face, preceded by burning pain. Which virus causes it?
q.e: Unilateral, dermatomal grouped vesicles after prodromal burning pain are shingles: reactivated varicella-zoster virus. The lesions stop at the midline.

q.r: Where to read more: Neville BW et al. Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology.

q.q: A 3-year-old boy is missing many primary teeth; those present are small and conical. He has sparse thin hair, dry skin, a prominent forehead, everted lips and heat intolerance from absent sweating. Testing shows an X-linked EDA mutation. What is the diagnosis and the first prosthetic management?
o: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia; early removable partial dentures or overdentures for chewing, speech and appearance
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome; bonded composite veneers only
q.e: Hypodontia with conical teeth, sparse hair and an inability to sweat is hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. Young children get removable dentures early, adjusted as they grow; implants wait until growth allows.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank

q.q: A 10-year-old has a complex impacted mesiodens, and a CBCT is considered. What is a main technical consideration and limitation of CBCT in children?
o: It can't be viewed on a monitor
A much higher dose than periapicals, and motion artifacts if the child moves
It can't show bone or teeth
It is contraindicated with amalgam fillings
q.e: CBCT gives a higher radiation dose than intraoral films, and children are more radiosensitive, so it is used only when 2D images can't answer the question. Scans take several seconds, so movement blurs the image.

q.q: A 7-year-old has delayed eruption of the permanent maxillary right central incisor. A panoramic radiograph shows a well-circumscribed radiopaque mass of many small tooth-like structures (denticles) above the crown. What is the diagnosis and management?
o: Compound odontoma; surgical excision to let the tooth erupt
q.e: Many small tooth-like denticles make a compound odontoma (a complex one is a shapeless mass). It is removed surgically so the blocked incisor can erupt.
q.c: Answer marked in the Dr. Fhd bank

q.q: A 19-year-old has an incidental well-defined radiolucency between vital mandibular incisors, with no symptoms. It looks like a simple (traumatic) bone cyst. What is the management?
q.e: A simple bone cyst is confirmed by surgical exploration: an empty cavity is found, and the bleeding caused by curetting the walls usually makes it heal.

q.q: A 52-year-old with good oral hygiene has a deeply stained occlusal fissure on 36 that is hard on probing, not sticky or soft, with no cavitation. Bitewings show no radiolucency and the tooth is symptom-free. What is the management?
q.e: A hard, stained, non-cavitated fissure with no radiographic caries in a low-risk adult is arrested or stained enamel, so it is left alone and monitored. Sealants are for at-risk fissures.

q.q: A 4-year-old with trauma to the primary maxillary central incisors won't hold a periapical receptor, so an anterior maxillary occlusal view with a size 2 receptor is taken. How are the head and beam positioned?
o: Head tilted back 45°; beam at +10° through the forehead
Occlusal plane tilted 90°; beam at −15° through the chin
Sagittal plane parallel to the floor; beam at 0°
Occlusal plane parallel to the floor; beam at +60° through the bridge of the nose
q.e: For the maxillary anterior occlusal view, the occlusal plane is parallel to the floor and the beam is aimed at about +60° through the tip/bridge of the nose toward the receptor.

q.q: A 28-year-old suddenly develops painful oral ulcers with crusted lip lesions and target-like skin lesions on the face and limbs over a few days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
q.e: Acute onset of oral ulcers, crusted bleeding lips and target (iris) skin lesions is erythema multiforme, often triggered by herpes simplex or drugs.

q.q: A 65-year-old with COPD and hypertension has a productive cough on the day of a routine appointment. BP is normal, pulse 80, oxygen saturation 90% on room air. What is the management?
q.e: A productive cough suggests an acute exacerbation or infection, and an SpO2 of 90% is low. Elective care is deferred until he is stable; when treated, COPD patients sit upright.

o: Return to work without reporting it
Report it to the responsible person at her workplace
Keep it private because it was accidental

q.q: About how much mercury vapor does a person with amalgam restorations absorb per day from chewing and eating?
q.e: Daily mercury absorption from amalgam fillings is about 1–3 µg, well below the level linked to any symptoms and less than what is taken in from food.

q.q: A 28-year-old wants ceramic crowns on 11 and 21 to replace discolored composites. She has high esthetic demands but wants to protect her long-term gum health; the sulcus is 1.5 mm and healthy. Which margin location best balances both?
q.e: Supragingival and equigingival margins are both well tolerated periodontally; subgingival margins carry the greatest biologic risk. With modern ceramics and resin cements, an equigingival margin blends in esthetically while staying healthy.
